title: Motivating People to Fully Engage
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article argues that even strong performers leave effort on the table and that leaders should work to unlock this discretionary effort, which the author likens to loose change in a pocket. The method is neither pressure nor expectation but involvement: leaders continually ask team members for views, ideas and solutions, including on strategy, competitors, market trends and metrics. This draws people into thinking about the enterprise beyond their daily tasks. The author claims full engagement follows from involvement and that people must feel ownership alongside the leader. The piece admits this demands planning, organization and time, and that not all leaders will commit. Its conclusion is that if full engagement is the goal, leaders have no other choice.
points: Discretionary effort is the gap between what people give and what they could give, and leaders can help them spend it.
Engagement results from involvement rather than expectation, so leaders keep asking for team members' thinking.
Inviting input on big-picture topics like strategy and competitors gets people thinking about the enterprise constantly.
The approach is labor-intensive for the leader, but the author argues there is no alternative if full engagement is the goal.
quotes: But even the highly ambitious and driven team members leave effort on the table. Performing at 100 percent all the time is a lofty goal, but nearly impossible to realize.
Discretionary effort is like loose change in the pocket. The best leaders work to help others spend that change to the benefit of the team. Every day.

How the best leaders create more engagement, more commitment, more effort, and more focus is not a secret. They’re continually asking others to engage with them. The best leaders lead by example by involving others in their engagement and commitment.

It encourages them to think about the enterprise all the time, not just during work hours. Full engagement and discretionary effort are a result of involvement, not expectation. When team members are fully involved, they become fully engaged.
Not all leaders will make this commitment. But if full engagement is the goal, team leaders have no other choice.

People need to own the enterprise or business with the leader to spend their discretionary time and effort thinking and acting to the benefit of the team. Effort jumps high whenever involvement sets the bar.
